nameStory: The Round-leaved Bog Orchid gets its name from its distinctive circular leaves that sit flat against the ground like green dinner plates. Unlike many orchids with narrow, grass-like leaves, this species shows off two perfectly round leaves that make it unmistakable among forest orchids. The 'bog' part of the name refers to its love of wet, mossy places, though it's equally happy in moist woodlands.
description: The Round-leaved Bog Orchid is a delicate woodland orchid that stands 1-2 feet tall when in bloom. Its most striking feature is a pair of large, perfectly circular leaves that lie flat on the ground like shiny green coins, each about 3-6 inches across. In summer, a single flower spike rises from between these leaves, bearing small greenish-white flowers arranged in a loose, airy cluster. This elegant orchid brings a touch of wild sophistication to New England's deep woods and wetlands.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two large, perfectly round leaves lying flat on the ground, glossy green and smooth to the touch, each about the size of your palm with prominent parallel veins running from base to tip

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small greenish-white flowers with a distinctive orchid shape, arranged loosely along a tall spike that rises 1-2 feet above the ground leaves, blooming in mid to late summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single plant with just two basal leaves and one flower stalk, often found scattered individually rather than in clusters

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, green flower stalk emerges directly from between the two round leaves, tall and slender with no leaves along its length

habitat: Look for Round-leaved Bog Orchids in cool, moist coniferous and mixed forests, especially where the ground stays consistently damp. They thrive in mossy areas under hemlocks, spruces, and firs, often near streams, seeps, or in the transition zones around bogs and swamps. In New England, they're most commonly found in the northern regions and higher elevations where the forest floor remains cool and humid.

seasonality.spring: The distinctive round leaves emerge and expand, lying flat against the mossy forest floor. This is actually the best time to spot them since the leaves are so distinctive and there's less competing vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom from July through August, sending up their elegant greenish-white flower spikes. The round leaves remain prominent and are often the first thing you'll notice.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may persist into early fall but begin to yellow and fade. Seeds develop in small capsules along the former flower spike.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. The plant survives underground until spring returns.

funFact: Despite being called a 'bog' orchid, this plant can live for decades in the same spot, with some individuals documented as being over 50 years old - making that pair of round leaves you're admiring possibly older than you are!
confusionNotes: The two perfectly round, flat leaves make this orchid nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. Hooker's Orchid also has two basal leaves, but they're much more oval and tend to stand upright rather than lying flat like dinner plates.
contextualKnowledge: Many people are surprised to learn that New England has wild orchids at all, thinking of orchids as tropical greenhouse plants. Our native orchids like this one are adapted to cool, temperate conditions and have much more subtle beauty than their showy tropical cousins.
compareHints: Among its bog orchid relatives, the Round-leaved Bog Orchid is unique for having just two large, circular basal leaves. Other Platanthera orchids in New England typically have several narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged up the stem, or if they have basal leaves, they're oval rather than perfectly round. The flat, plate-like arrangement of the leaves also sets it apart from Hooker's Orchid, whose similar two-leaf pattern consists of upright, oval leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bog orchid relatives, this is by far the smallest and most inconspicuous - while cousins like the fringed orchids have showy white or purple flowers, the small green wood orchid is all about stealth.

Among its Platanthera relatives, the White-fringed Orchid is distinguished by its pure white color and deeply fringed petals - the Lesser and Greater Purple Fringed Orchids have similar fringed flowers but are purple, while other white bog orchids lack the dramatic fringe.
Among New England's bog orchids (Platanthera), the Lesser Purple Fringed Orchid is distinguished by its bright purple color and deeply fringed flower lips.
White bog orchid stands out from its Platanthera relatives by its pure white color and incredibly strong clove-like fragrance.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the ragged fringed orchid stands out for its greenish-white color and extremely irregular, deeply cut fringes.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the Greater Purple Fringed Orchid stands out for its size and deeply fringed purple petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this species is distinguished by its greenish-white flowers and self-fertilizing habit.
Among its bog orchid relatives, green bog orchid is distinguished by its consistently greenish flowers and preference for the wettest habitats.
Among New England's bog orchids, pale green orchid stands out for its particularly subtle coloring and preference for disturbed shoreline habitats.

Among New England's bog orchids, Hooker's is distinctive for having exactly two large basal leaves lying flat on the ground, while most other Platanthera species have multiple leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, Large-leaved Bog Orchid is unmistakable due to its two massive basal leaves - most other Platanthera species have smaller, more numerous leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the orange-fringed orchid is the only one with orange flowers and deeply fringed petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this is the only one with such intensely bright orange flowers in a dense, compact cluster.

Unlike its relatives the round-leaved bog orchid (which has two large round leaves) or Hooker's orchid (which has two broad leaves that hug the ground), the blunt-leaved rein orchid typically has just one distinctively paddle-shaped leaf with a rounded tip.
Among its Platanthera relatives, Shriver's frilly orchid is distinguished by its particular fringe pattern and purple coloration.
